1.7.24.en: It is fitting for us to take care that our love for God is not for the sake of a reward. For what kind of reward is this that God gives you?

1.7.25.en: Whatever He gives you is less than Himself. Do not worship God in order to receive something from Him. Worship Him without hoping for anything in return, and then you will receive Him, for God keeps Himself for you to enjoy.

1.7.26.en: If you love what He created, how much more is the Creator of the world? Remove from your heart the love of creatures, that you may cleave to the Creator, and then you will say what is in the Psalm: [It is good for me to cleave to my God] (Ps 73:28).

1.7.27.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Satan says, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Why do you marvel at Job? Why do you make extraordinary declarations about an upright man? For you yourself insist on his righteousness, and this only because of your gifts, which he received with great generosity in return for his virtue. He has abundance in everything; he is glutted with everything; he has no anxiety, nothing that makes him sin. His house is well built, full of good things. All his possessions are fenced with a hedge of blessings. His sons surround him like a crown that crowns him. Why should Job not be upright? Why should he not be godly? Which commandment is he bound to neglect? For he who has never tasted poverty, why should he steal?

1.7.28.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * With impudence he entered into an argument with God (Job 1:9). This is not the attitude of Satan alone, but of wicked men. Did not the one of whom it is said in the Gospel do the same: "I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed" (Mt 24:25)...

1.7.29.en: He was seeking to distort Job's motive... God always wishes to pronounce His judgment from the words of His enemies, so as to leave them no room for any excuse, as it is said in the passage: "Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant" (Lk 22:19)... By this deceit is always caught in its own net.

1.7.30.en: St. John Chrysostom "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?

1.7.31.en: Thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land!" [10].

1.7.32.en: Rabbi Yose b. Hanina concluded from (Job 1:10) that Job's goats were able to kill wolves. And R. Yohanan concluded from (Job 1:14) that God granted Job to taste paradisal life, so Satan envied him, and began to fight him, slandering him concerning his righteousness.

1.7.33.en: Satan puts the blame on God: "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?" Truly God had set a hedge around him for the protection of him and his house, and granted him success and wealth, and blessed his works, but He did not do this out of partiality, for Job was not characterized by dullness and slackness.

1.7.34.en: The speech of Satan reveals that he expended every effort to find a gap through which to enter Job's heart or mind in order to draw him into his kingdom, but he found none.

1.7.35.en: * "Because thou hast said, Thou, O Lord, art my refuge; thou hast made the most High thy habitation" (Ps 91:9). In order to enjoy this divine care he says: Experience hope in the Lord, and make Him a refuge for yourself... "There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling" (Ps 91:10). You will stand firm before the darts of Satan, and they will not hurt you at all. Thus divine grace was set around Job's house, which the enemy bore witness to, crying out in a loud voice: "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house?" And when He permitted him (to tempt him), He showed on the other side his wickedness, and the just Judge crowned the victorious wrestler.

1.7.36.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * "Hast not thou made an hedge about him?" Do you not notice that even Satan fully realizes that all of Job's security comes from God? He says, "Thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land." Do you not see that his wealth is a gift from God? Do you not see that it is not the fruit of injustice (or seizure)...?

1.7.37.en: "But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will bless thee to thy face (that is, curse thee)" [11]. He wanted and desired to receive this authority from Him, but he did not dare to say it.

1.7.38.en: * What is God's own work, if not this: to do good to all humanity, by chastisements as well as by pleasures? Let us then give thanks not only when we are in prosperity, for this is nothing great. This too Satan knows well; therefore he said: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about all that he hath on every side?" (Job 1:9-10)

1.7.39.en: St. John Chrysostom * Blessed David knows that this temporary abandonment on God's part toward us is sometimes for our good, and in his prayer he asked that it not be continual (for he knows that God's abandoning man is harmful, since human nature is unable to walk toward perfection); therefore he besought that it be within certain limits, saying: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 8:119). In other words he says: I know that You forsake Your saints for their benefit, to test them... Therefore I do not ask You not to forsake me, for it is not beneficial for me not to feel my weakness [therefore he said, "It is good for me that I have been humbled" (Ps 119:71)], nor is it useful for me not to have the opportunity for battle. And this opportunity will certainly not be available to me as long as I am filled with the constant protection of God. For Satan does not dare to fight me as long as I rely on Your protection, so he comes forward objecting and complaining against me and against You: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?" (Job 1:9-10). I ask You to forsake me, but "not utterly" (the Greek word is "not much"), because it is useful for me that You forsake me a little, so that the steadfastness of my love may be tested.

1.7.40.en: Fr. Daniel * Your words strike me hard in my chest, and make a hedge around me on every side.

1.7.41.en: St. Augustine "But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face" [11].

1.7.42.en: In a discourse of Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, on divine providence, he raised the objection of some: Why do the majority of the rich live a life marked by injustice? Why do they not seek justice? Perhaps he drew such an objection from Philo of Alexandria and from some of the Stoics. Theodoret answers: [Again, you forget that man has a free will. By this you deprive him of the glory that was given to him by his Maker. Besides this, evildoers would find a strong ground for defending themselves if the Judge distributed wealth to the righteous alone in the present life. They would say what their master said about Job: "Thou hast made a hedge about them and about their houses. Thou hast multiplied their crops and their vineyards. But put forth thine hand now and touch all that they have, and they will bless (that is, curse) thee to thy face." This is what hardened sinners would say if the practicers of virtue alone received the gift of wealth.]

1.7.43.en: St. Augustine sees that the true believer, like Job, is a stretched-out trumpet, and that trials are like beating with a hammer; when it strikes the trumpet it gives forth joyful sounds of praise. So the hammer that shatters the unbeliever reveals the peace and rejoicing of the believer, and so commends him before God.

1.7.44.en: * If it were in his power, would (Satan) not take vengeance for himself? But he is not permitted to do so. When he wished to tempt Job, he asked to receive authority to do so, and he was not able to do anything he had not received authority for. So why do you not worship God without fear, He without whom no one will harm you, and by whose permission you are disciplined but not defeated?

1.7.45.en: * (Satan) was able to envy the holy man (Job), but was he able to harm him?

1.7.46.en: He could accuse him, but was he able to condemn him?

1.7.47.en: Was he able to take anything from him or harm him, even the size of a fingernail or a hair of his head, without saying to God: "Put forth thine hand"?

1.7.48.en: Give me authority. It was given to him.

1.7.49.en: One tempted, and the other was tempted. But the one who was tempted conquered, and the one who tempted was defeated.

1.7.50.en: So God, who permitted Satan to take away all that he had, did not forsake him inwardly, as his servant. He made the very soul of His servant a sword by which Satan was defeated.

1.7.51.en: And what is the result? I think that it is for the benefit of humanity in general. The man who was defeated in paradise became a victor on the dunghill. In one place the devil defeated him through a woman, and in another place he conquered the devil and the woman together.

1.7.52.en: St. Augustine * Satan prepares the temptation; if he sees a person who is weak he attacks him, but if he sees him strong he stops.

1.7.53.en: St. John Chrysostom * This also we read of: that divine righteousness truly helped faithful Job in his wrestling, when Satan opposed him in a unique battle. But if Job had advanced against his enemy, not by his own strength but under the protection of God's grace, supported by divine help without exercising any endurance on his part, then in his submission to these many trials... Satan would have been able to speak with justice, slandering with what he had said before: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him... about all that he hath on every side? But put forth thine hand now," that is, permit me to fight him, "and he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 1:9-11).

1.7.54.en: But the slandering enemy could not make this protest after the battle, because he was defeated by the strength of Job and not by the strength of God; not in the sense that God's grace forsook Job, for it was what gave the tempter authority to tempt within the limits in which it saw that Job could resist, and at the same time grace did not protect him from the enemy's attacks in a way that removed his virtue and his striving, but rather helped him. That is, it does not permit that enemy, who is extremely cruel, to take away his mind or to drown him in his weakness by instilling thoughts beyond his strength, or to descend with him into a contest unequal to him.

1.7.55.en: Fr. Chaeremon * Divine providence often permits the believer to face afflictions, but this shows others the virtue hidden in him; so it was in the case of Job.

1.7.56.en: Fr. John of Damascus "And the LORD said unto Satan,

1.7.57.en: Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand.

1.7.58.en: So Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD" [12].

1.7.59.en: God permitted Satan to tempt Job, as He permitted him to sift Peter the Apostle, but He took care that his faith should not fail (Lk 22:32), for trials turn to praise and honor and glory (1 Pet 1:7).

1.7.60.en: The permission that the Lord granted to Satan gives the believer reassurance and peace, for the enemy of good cannot touch a believer without the permission of his God, nor can he even approach his possessions without the permission of his God. God is the almighty, loving, wise Father, who gives permission to the extent that we can bear, and in a way that turns to our glory if we are faithful.

1.7.61.en: It is said of the enemy of good, "Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD," as it was said of Cain (Gen 4:16), since evil cannot bear to exist in the divine presence. But of the sons of God who stand before God it is not said that they went forth from the presence of the Lord. So believers remain in the presence of the Lord even in their moments of sleep!

1.7.62.en: God permitted Satan to receive authority to tempt righteous Job within the limits He set for him. Here Pope Gregory (the Great) distinguishes between Satan's will and his authority. As for his will, it is always evil; but his authority that is permitted him by God will contain no injustice, because it is by divine permission for our proving and edification. For this reason we do not wonder at what is stated in (1 Sam 10:18): "The evil spirit from God came violently upon Saul, and he raved in the midst of the house." He is an evil spirit, but the saying "from God" is because he could not have rushed upon Saul without receiving authority from the just God. St. Paul says: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" (1 Cor 13:10). Therefore David the psalmist says: "Prove me, O Lord, and try me" (Ps 2:26).

1.7.63.en: St. Augustine sees that God permits Satan to bring afflictions upon them, either for their discipline, as He delivered His people to captivity by strangers; or for testing so that they may be proved, as He permitted Job to be tempted; or to send them forward to receive the crown, as He permitted martyrs to be persecuted.

1.7.64.en: *In truth, when Satan asked to be given authority against Job, his attack on him was the cause of Job's receiving double glory after his victory. His receiving twice what he lost in the present showed in truth that he will without doubt receive in the same way in the heavenly places. The Apostle says: "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2 Tim 2:5).

1.7.65.en: In truth, how can there be striving if there is no one to resist?

1.7.66.en: How great is the beauty and splendor of the light, which cannot be discerned unless the darkness of night stands against it.

1.7.67.en: Why are some praised for purity, if not because others are condemned for their impudence?

1.7.68.en: Why are the strong glorified, if not because there are cowards?

1.7.69.en: When you make use of what is bitter, then the sweet becomes all the more worthy of praise for you.

1.7.70.en: Origen * We read in the Book of Job how Satan himself, who appears to have all authority for a time, cannot do anything without permission. He received authority over lower things, and lost his authority over everything greater and higher. This authority of his is not like that of one who issues a penalty, but the penalty rests upon himself.

1.7.71.en: * God permitted the tempter, not that He might know what He already knows (about Job), but that we might know and imitate him. He delivered him to the tempter, and everything was taken away. And the man remained stripped of his possessions and of his family and of his children, but he was full of God.

1.7.72.en: * The tempter was permitted to tempt a holy man, Job. In one moment he took away all things, removed all that he possessed, took away the inheritance, and killed the heirs. This did not happen little by little, but all together, in one blow... He announced it all in a sudden announcement. When everything was removed, Job alone remained, but there remained in him the vows of praise which he offers to God.

1.7.73.en: * God granted (His people) their request, and gave them a king after their heart, as it is written, and not after His own heart. He also granted what Satan asked of Him, to tempt His servant that he might be proved.

1.7.74.en: St. Augustine * Do you not see the limits that were set in the test? Do you not notice that Satan could not even touch the flock if he had not received authority?

1.7.75.en: St. John Chrysostom * The tempter Satan is permitted to stir up war against the saints by every means of temptation, so that their love for God may be proved, and that it may be a witness. This is when things are taken away from them, or they are deprived, or become in want and destitute of sensible things, while they remain lovers of God, steadfast in His love, loving in truth. And while (Satan) tries to entice them, they remain undefeated, and do not change their love for God...

1.7.76.en: For the enemy strongly desires to tempt every man, if that were possible for him, and asks God on behalf of all to tempt them, as he asked on behalf of the righteous man Job... And when he received permission in a short time, Satan approached immediately according to the strength of the one he would tempt. So the evil one struggles with them according to his desire. By these means, those who are upright and steadfast in the love of God are proved when they scorn everything and count it as nothing beside their love for God.

1.7.77.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Authority against us is given in two forms, either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are proved, as we see in the case of Job.

1.7.78.en: Cyprian the Martyr * "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand" [12], can have another meaning. The Lord truly knew that His soldier was courageous, and that victory was certain under all circumstances for this steadfast wrestler. And that the enemy would return to the Lord defeated from one struggle. Then He permits him another battle so that he may be defeated once more, and the one who follows Him faithfully becomes all the more incomparably victorious over the defeated enemy who has regained his strength for new wars.

1.7.80.en: *What is written about Job is not without meaning, for it is clear from the Scripture that Satan asked for him and sought him. For Satan cannot do anything of himself without permission from God.

1.7.81.en: What does Satan say to the Lord? "Deliver him into my hand, for he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 1:11). And Job is still as he was until now, and so is God, and so also is Satan. Therefore, to that extent Satan seeks him and says to the Lord: [He serves You only because You help him and protect him and support him; but put forth Your hand now and deliver him to me, and he will curse You to Your face.]

1.7.82.en: In short, when a person has obtained consolation by grace, grace withdraws a little so that he may be delivered to trials. And Satan comes and brings with him thousands of evils as temptations for the man, such as despair, apostasy and evil thoughts, to torment the soul with them, in order to weaken it and separate it from hope in the Lord.

1.7.83.en: St. Macarius the Great *[Lead us not into temptation]. The prayer here is not that we may not be tried, but that we may not enter (be led) into temptation. For since every man must be tested by fire, he should pray not that the fire may not touch him, but that he may not perish. For vessels of clay are tested by the furnace, and man is tested by afflictions, trail of tribulation (Sir 27:6)(a).

1.7.84.en: Joseph was tested by the temptation of fornication, but he did not enter into temptation (Gen 7:39-12).

1.7.85.en: And Susanna was also tried without entering into temptation (Addition to Dan 13:22).

1.7.86.en: And many of both sexes were tried without entering into temptation.

1.7.87.en: But Job was the greatest of them, for he stood with wonderful steadfastness in the Lord his God.

1.7.88.en: St. Augustine * (The demons) have no authority nor power to exercise against anyone unless they receive permission from God according to His plan, such as what happened against Job (Job 1:12), and against the swine mentioned in the Gospels (Mk 5:13).

1.7.89.en: Fr. John of Damascus * The evil spirits have no authority to harm anyone; this is clearly shown in the case of the blessed Job, where the enemy did not dare to tempt him except as God permitted... The spirits themselves confessed this, as it is in the Gospel, for they said, "If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine" (Mt 31:8). If they have no authority to enter the unclean dumb animals except by permission from God, how much less are they able to enter man, who is created in the image of God?!

1.8.0.en: 13 And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house: 14 And there came a messenger unto Job, and said, The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them: 15 And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 16 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 17 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 18 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house: 19 And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.

1.8.1.en: "And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house" [13].

1.8.2.en: * We must notice the timing at which the trials came. Satan chose the time of the temptation when the sons of blessed Job were occupied in a feast (Job 1:13). The adversary did not search only for what to do, but for when to do it. Although he had received permission, he sought the suitable time to carry out his destruction. And by God's arrangement the purpose was to record this for our benefit, for the enjoyment of complete pleasures is a preparation for the coming of calamities.

1.8.4.en: "And there came a messenger unto Job, and said,

1.9.0.en: The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them" [14].

1.9.1.en: In the Septuagint it says "the she asses with their young." With great cunning the enemy wanted to increase the bitterness of the calamity: the Sabeans carried off the useful oxen, since they were plowing the land, and the she asses that were fruitful, since their young were with them. By this the enemy wanted to strike violently, to make the wound in the soul of righteous Job more bitter. Besides this, the calamities fell one after another with extreme speed.

1.10.0.en: And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee [15].

1.10.1.en: When Satan took permission to tempt, he did not lack the will with which to carry out his plan, for the wicked fulfil the counsel of their wicked father. As the Lord Christ said to the Jews of His time: "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do" (Jn 8:44). For he is "the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Eph 2:2).

1.10.2.en: * Do you not see the swiftness of the blow...? Nothing like this had ever happened before, nor had anyone heard of such a thing. Add to this that it was no longer possible to plow the land, and in a moment Job was stripped of all his possessions. The sight of the destruction of a flock is always painful, especially if it happens at a time when a man depends entirely upon it... Add to that the occurrence of killing in the midst of the devastation, which makes the struggle unbearable, as brutality and savagery appear. It is a double calamity, killing and raiding expeditions, with the remaining emaciation added to the afflictions that befell him, so that it no longer left him ignorant of the dreadful nature of the calamity of the event.

1.10.3.en: St. John Chrysostom St. Ambrose affirms that many things that seem evil and wicked, and from which we suffer, become an opportunity for the growth of our virtues, as happened with Job in his many trials.

1.10.4.en: * Would (Job) not have been in a less blessed state if he had not suffered these things by which in truth he was proved?

1.10.5.en: St. Ambrose "While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,

1.11.0.en: The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [16].

1.11.1.en: The calamities followed one another in moments and with extreme speed, and perhaps the enemy did so deliberately so as not to leave Job an opportunity for balanced thought, but with the successive disasters he would think that God's wrath had come down upon him and would not stop. The trials were like waves that never subside. "Deep calleth unto deep" (Ps 42:7).

1.11.2.en: What is remarkable about the messengers coming to Job is that they affirm that the oxen were plowing and the asses feeding. As though even the animals were doing their part, so that there is no blame on the sons, nor the servants, nor the animals, and as though all the blame falls on God alone and no one else. Satan's plan was extremely well devised, to strike Job's heart so as to turn all his feelings and thoughts toward blaspheming God.

1.11.3.en: While I was writing down this interpretation, a young man suddenly died, and his friend, who was very dear to him, began to blaspheme: "Why did God take the dearest friend I have?" and he refuses any consolation... and sometimes he even mutters: "Where is God? And if He exists, where is His mercy and His care?" As though the enemy of good in every generation expends every effort to turn the energies of humanity toward blaspheming God.

1.11.4.en: The enemy of good did not give Job the opportunity to think of waging war against the Sabeans and recovering his possessions, for the next news came announcing that a fire from heaven had come down from God and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them. If he wanted to fight the Sabeans, from where would he bring his men to fight, when a divine fire had burned them up? And then, would he fight God? And how could he reach Him...? It was as though nothing remained within Job's reach but his tongue to blaspheme God as a violent oppressor who knows no mercy.

1.11.5.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that by saying, "The fire of God is fallen from heaven," the enemy wanted to suggest to Job that what befell him was not human blows but from God, and directed against him alone and not the rest of those around him. Perhaps by this he wanted to distort the image of God in his eyes. For although he had committed no great sins and had not been negligent in worshipping God, yet God had come down in His wrath upon him and no one else, which stirs in him the motive to blaspheme God as unjust. Since God burned up the sheep, of which he had chosen the best to offer as burnt offerings to God, God appears as One who is not pleased with his burnt offerings and does not accept his worship, or as though "it is vain to serve God" (Mal 3:14).

1.11.6.en: Nothing had been heard of burning coming from heaven since the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah; therefore Job says: [For destruction from the LORD was a terror to me] (Job 31:23).

1.11.7.en: * Lest the loss of his possessions should not stir him to sufficient grief when he heard the news, he spurred on his feelings with the very words of the messenger.

1.11.8.en: Notice how cunningly it was said "the fire of God," as if to say that you are suffering from a visitation of the One whom you want to appease with so many sacrifices. Behold, you have fallen under the wrath of the One whose service you busy yourself with every day...

1.11.9.en: This is the aim: that he should recall to his memory his past services, and reckon that he had served in vain, as though he wanted to stir up in him the feeling of the Creator's injustice.

1.11.10.en: For the godly mind, finding itself facing the bearing of crosses at the hands of a man, seeks consolations from divine providence. And when it sees the storm of temptation drawing its strength from outside, it seeks to cover it with trust in the Lord, and takes refuge inwardly in the harbor of conscience. But that cunning adversary wanted at that very moment to break the heart of this brave saint, by blows directed from a man and by despair of God.

1.11.11.en: He came to him with news first of the Sabeans who had carried out the plunder, and immediately the report came of the fire of God that fell from heaven, so as to close the door completely to any means of consolation.

1.11.13.en: "While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,

1.12.0.en: The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [17].

1.12.1.en: The enemy did not leave him to think why the fire fell from heaven as though by divine command, for another messenger came to him telling him of a new blow by the deed of the Chaldeans. In this he wants to confuse Job's mind. For if the fire had come down from God, Job might think that it was a blow to discipline him, but when he finds that even men fall upon him, how will he justify this?

1.12.2.en: For the third time a grave calamity befalls him, and it came by way of three bands of Chaldeans, at a time when Job had lost every possibility of resistance. Perhaps the enemy wanted by this blow that Job should cry out in his heart: "Why does the Lord make the way of the wicked prosper?"

1.12.3.en: "While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,

1.13.0.en: Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house" [18].

1.14.0.en: "And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [19].

1.14.1.en: To increase the bitterness of the calamity, he sent him grave news, that nature too was in revolt against him, for a great wind shook the house and killed his sons and daughters, so that it would be hard for him to bring out their bodies whole! Their appearance would be extremely hideous. Besides this, to confuse Job's mind: how do heaven and earth join together against him, God and men and nature resisting him, why? What had he done to fall under these successive calamities from different sources?

1.14.2.en: This, the most grievous of the blows, the enemy left to the end, so as to aim a deadly arrow at Job's heart, for his sons and daughters all died in moments under the rubble. It is an extremely grave loss. When David's infant son fell ill, he could not bear the bitterness, but went to and fro crying out; what then of Job, who lost all his sons and daughters suddenly.

1.14.3.en: Job needed his children to comfort him in all that he had lost, but their death, especially in this way, surely made him forget all the previous trials and fall into unbearable bitterness.

1.14.4.en: St. John Chrysostom says that in the previous calamities there may be justification for the messenger's saying: "and I only am escaped alone," since he escaped what befell Job's animals; but that this last messenger should escape the fall of the house while all Job's sons and daughters die together is unnatural, so what is the secret? Chrysostom sees that this messenger was not a man but Satan himself, for how could one who served Job's sons and daughters escape without them, while he was with them in the same house that fell and destroyed those in it?

1.14.5.en: * Have you lost a child! Have you not lost him? Do not say this; he is asleep, not dead; he has moved and has not been destroyed; he is on a journey from a bad state to a better one.

1.14.6.en: Do not provoke God to anger, but entreat Him. For if you bear this nobly, the rest is doubled for the departed as well as for you. But if the opposite happens, you inflame God's wrath all the more...

1.14.7.en: Give thanks, for by this the cloud of grief is dispersed from you. Say with Job: [The LORD hath given, the LORD hath taken away] (Job 21:1).

1.15.0.en: 20 Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped, 21 And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. 22 In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.

1.15.1.en: "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped" [20].

1.15.2.en: Had Job not behaved thus he would have been counted a man dull of feeling, rigid, unnatural and foolish, unmoved by the death of his sons and servants. By this behavior he revealed the bitterness of his soul without going beyond the bounds of propriety, in view of the multitude of the successive trials and their hideousness.

1.15.3.en: Besides this, what he did was in keeping with the customs followed at that time. His behavior does not mean that he lost his inner peace or his courage and patience and power of endurance.

1.15.4.en: Some commentators see that he had recourse to this because the enemy of good tried to instill thoughts of blasphemy against God. So the tearing of clothes and the shaving of the head are a sign of his insistence on rejecting these thoughts. For the tearing of clothes is a sign of the desire to reject blasphemy, as the high priest did when he thought that Jesus Christ had blasphemed.

1.15.5.en: His prostration to the ground is a sign of his sincerity with himself, as he felt that he was a sinner and that his soul had been brought down to the dust.

1.15.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job tore his clothes and shaved the hair of his head because of grief, but more so in order to strip himself of everything, even his garment and the hair of his head, so that the enemy of good would find nothing in which he could tempt him. And in humility before God he fell to the ground.

1.15.7.en: * He "worshipped" to convince the traitor that he slanders him in vain before God. For the one of whom he (Satan) said that he would blaspheme (Job 11:1; 5:2), behold, he worships. The person of whom he said that when his possessions were destroyed he would show ingratitude before God, behold, he gives thanks more than before.

1.15.8.en: * Some count it a high degree of the philosophy of steadfastness that when they fall under severe discipline they are dull in their feeling of the blows and in the pain of the scourgings. And some exaggerate their sensitivity to the pain of the blows...

1.15.9.en: The prophet says: "Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction" (Jer 3:5). In contrast to this, concerning the inward dialogue in the feeling of discipline, the psalmist says: "They shall not stand firm in the trial" (Ps 140:10) (Vulgate). For they stand firm in the trial if they bear it with patience.

1.15.10.en: * It was the custom in ancient times that each one kept up his personal appearance by letting his hair grow, to cut it in times of grief.

1.15.11.en: When the holy man lost everything in the time of his trial through the adversary, he realized that Satan has no authority to tempt him without the permission of the Lord; therefore he did not say: "The Lord gave, and Satan took away"... For it would be sad if what the Creator gives were taken away from him by the enemy. But the one who takes it is none other than the One who gave, who took back what was His and did not take what is ours. For everything we use in our present life comes from Him, so why should we grieve if we return to Him what we borrowed from Him through His generosity?

1.15.13.en: * O the courage of Job, which surpasses all that is told! O the humility! O the love of God...!

1.15.14.en: Did the enemy think that Job did not care about the oxen, and was not concerned about the she asses, and counted the flock a thing of no value, and the camels as though they were nothing, and all his possessions things to be despised?

1.15.15.en: What about the grief over the death of his sons and daughters, how did it not cast him into terror...?

1.15.16.en: He who was the father of many children no longer had anyone to call him "my father."

1.15.17.en: He did not say to God: "What many sins has Job committed, that he should be counted unworthy to embrace his children at their death, and not be able to honor them by burying them in a tomb, nor be able to be comforted with tears as a fully natural custom, nor be able to lead a funeral procession, as fathers and friends usually do...?"

1.15.18.en: Then I wish you would not be angry when you are stripped of your possessions, and deprived of temporal honors, and separated from sons or fathers.

1.15.19.en: When you lose them according to the law of nature, do not be troubled...

1.15.20.en: For your true wealth, which is the praise of God, cannot be taken away from you, a thing that makes you strong to defy all events.

1.15.21.en: Does the servant bring an accusation when he is asked for the talents that his master entrusted to him? (Mt 19:25)

1.15.22.en: Or when he has taken a loan, is he troubled when he returns it...?

1.15.23.en: Yes, since we give what is not ours, let us come before God as One worthy of thanks, when He gives as when He takes.

1.15.24.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head" [20]. Do not think, beloved, that this gesture is a sign of defeat; rather it is especially a sign of victory. For if he had not acted at all, he would have been thought to be in a state of stupor, but he truly showed himself wise and a godly father at the same time. For what a loss this was that befell him! He did not grieve only over the loss of his sons and also his animals, but over the way in which they died. Who is not shattered before these events? What man of iron is not moved by them?

1.15.25.en: Paul also had these feelings in the face of tears, for he says: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart?" (Acts 13:21) and by this he was an object of admiration! So Job is worthy of admiration, because despite the feelings that drove him to this movement, he expressed them in a way in which there was nothing unseemly at all...

1.15.26.en: Moses (the prophet) broke (the tablets of the Law), and Joshua tore his clothes (Ex 15:32-20; Josh 6:7); if Job had not torn his clothes it would have been said that God created him with an unfeeling (rigid) nature, but he accepted the sufferings that befall the righteous so that you may realize that he was bound to be wise even in his grief.

1.15.27.en: * "And fell down upon the ground, and worshipped" [20]. Lest you think that his tearing of his clothes means blasphemy, and that he is in a state of anger at the events, listen to what he says. He yielded his garment to Satan. The text says: "And shaved his head... and said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." Again he speaks well. For from that time he faces the struggle, casting himself naked.

1.15.28.en: He fell to the ground and made Satan fall. He showed his feelings and made clear his godliness...

1.15.29.en: Notice how by these actions he proclaimed the words of the Apostle: "For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Tim 7:6).

1.15.30.en: Notice how the words he uttered served him, not he alone, but will serve us also.

1.15.31.en: These possessions above all, are they mine? Am I the one who formed them?

1.15.32.en: This wealth, is it not a deposit? It is foreign to me, for it did not accompany me when I entered this world, and it does not accompany me when I depart...

1.15.33.en: Let us be dull toward wealth. For this reason God created us naked from the beginning, and made us subject to death.

1.15.34.en: St. John Chrysostom * When Job's sons died, they found a common grave under the rubble of his house, and all he could do was show his fatherly affection by tearing his clothes and falling on the ground and worshipping, saying: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:20).

1.15.35.en: St. Jerome "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither.

1.16.0.en: The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" [21].

1.16.1.en: The Holy Bible does not mention any hymn of praise sung by Adam and Eve in paradise amid all the surpassing gifts and blessings they enjoyed. But the Book of Job has recorded for us a short hymn that surpasses many hymns, a hymn that gladdens the heart of God and the hearts of the heavenly beings, and remains engraved as on rock, sung by the generations, and in which people through the generations find divine comfort. So we would not have enjoyed the Psalms and the life of inward rejoicing if David the prophet had not been a man of sorrows, and we would not sing the hymn of the three holy youths if they had not been thrown into the furnace of fire.

1.16.2.en: By saying this Job declares his return to his origin, and as the wise man says: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was" (Eccl 12:7). Naked we return, when we go back to the dust from which we were taken (Job 34:15). The Latin proverb says that "no one can reach a state of poverty more extreme than that in which he was born."

1.16.3.en: Job's faithfulness appeared contrary to what Satan claimed, for instead of blaspheming God he blessed Him, acknowledging divine providence whatever afflictions befell him.

1.16.4.en: He did not say, God gave and the Sabeans and Chaldeans took away, nor did he say, God gave to me and the Lord impoverished me, but said that God who gave has the right to take. He lost nothing, for all that he has, even his children, belong to God; they are His gift.

1.16.5.en: He blessed God who gave, and blesses Him because He took, for the remaining of the gifts, even for a time, is an expression of God's love for us. And because God, who is all-wise, all-loving and almighty, knows what is for our edification and to the extent that is for our benefit, even the taking from us is for our good.

1.16.6.en: * When the messengers came to blessed Job one after another, and he heard them announcing deadly news, with the unbearable destruction of his sons added to it, he did not cry out or sigh, but had recourse to prayer and offered thanks to the Lord; imitate him.
